title: Akkad and the Third Dynasty of Ur
subtitle: 2334–2004 BC · The First Empire, the God-King Naram-Sin, the Gutian Interlude, and the Bureaucratic Renaissance of Ur

categories.label: Power
categories.subtitle: Sargon's Akkad and the first empire, the self-deification of Naram-Sin, the Gutian interlude and Gudea's Lagash, and the bureaucratic renaissance and swift fall of the Third Dynasty of Ur

entries.label: Sargon founds the first empire
entries.hint: Sargon rose as cup-bearer to the king of Kish, seized power, and built a new capital, Akkad, whose site has never been found. He defeated Lugalzagesi and the kings of Sumer, campaigned to the cedar mountains and the Mediterranean, washed his weapons in the Lower Sea, and installed his daughter Enheduanna as priestess at Ur. He ruled the whole of Mesopotamia for over fifty years — the first man to weld it into one state and hold it.
entries.note: Douglas Frayne, RIME 2 (1993); Benjamin Foster, 'The Age of Agade' (2016); the later 'Sargon Birth Legend' edited by Brian Lewis (1980).

entries.label: Rimush and Manishtushu — revolt and consolidation
entries.hint: Sargon's sons inherited a rebellion. Rimush put down a general Sumerian revolt with a slaughter his own inscriptions tally by the tens of thousands, and was then murdered by his courtiers. Manishtushu raided across the Gulf against thirty-two kings of Magan and left an obelisk recording enormous royal purchases of land — the crown turning conquest into permanent estates.
entries.note: Frayne, RIME 2 (1993); the Manishtushu Obelisk (Louvre) in Gelb, Steinkeller & Whiting, 'Earliest Land Tenure Systems in the Near East' (1991).

entries.label: Naram-Sin, god of Akkad
entries.hint: Naram-Sin, Sargon's grandson, crushed a 'Great Revolt' of Kish, Uruk and a wide coalition, claiming nine battles won in a single year. In its wake the citizens of Akkad asked the gods to make him their city-god: he wrote his name with the sign for 'divine', wore the horned crown of a deity, and styled himself 'King of the Four Quarters'. He campaigned from Anatolia to Magan and destroyed Ebla and Armanum in Syria.
entries.note: Frayne, RIME 2 (1993); the deification analysed in Piotr Michalowski, 'The Mortal Kings of Ur' (2008); the 'Great Revolt' text in Old Babylonian copies (Aage Westenholz).

entries.label: Shar-kali-sharri and the unravelling
entries.hint: Shar-kali-sharri dropped the grand title and called himself simply 'king of Akkad'. He fought the Gutians in the Zagros, the Elamites in the east and the Amorites in the west, and rebuilt the Ekur at Nippur. After him the empire dissolved into a scramble the King List records as a bitter question: 'Who was king? Who was not king?'
entries.note: Frayne, RIME 2 (1993); the interregnum in the Sumerian King List (Jacobsen 1939) and Foster, 'The Age of Agade' (2016).

entries.label: The Gutians hold the land
entries.loc: the Zagros piedmont and the central plain
entries.hint: A people from the Zagros mountains, the Gutians raided the collapsing empire and then loosely dominated its centre and north for two or three generations. Later Sumerian texts cast them as barbarians 'who knew no inhibitions', and blame them for ruin and famine. How much they actually governed is unclear — many southern cities, Lagash above all, ran their own affairs and prospered.
entries.note: W. W. Hallo, 'Gutium' (Reallexikon der Assyriologie III); the hostile tradition in 'The Curse of Agade' (Cooper 1983) and the Utu-hegal inscription.

entries.label: Gudea of Lagash, the builder
entries.hint: While the north lay under the Gutians, Lagash under its governor Gudea was independent and rich, trading for cedar from the Amanus, diorite from Magan and copper and carnelian from farther still. Gudea spent his reign rebuilding the temple of Ningirsu, the Eninnu, an undertaking he recorded on two great clay cylinders — the longest Sumerian literary text — and commemorated in some two dozen statues of himself carved from imported black stone.
entries.note: Dietz Otto Edzard, RIME 3/1: 'Gudea and His Dynasty' (1997); the Cylinders translated in Thorkild Jacobsen, 'The Harps That Once...' (1987).

entries.label: Utu-hegal drives out the Gutians
entries.hint: Utu-hegal, king of Uruk, marched against the Gutian king Tirigan, defeated and captured him, and 'set his foot on his neck' — ending, in his own telling, the kingship of Gutium and returning it to Sumer. His victory inscription is the main source for the episode. He reigned only a few years before his own appointed governor of Ur, Ur-Namma, eclipsed him.
entries.note: The Utu-hegal inscription in Frayne, RIME 2 (1993); Jacob Klein, 'Šulgi and Išme-Dagan' and studies of the Uruk V dynasty.

entries.label: Ur-Namma founds the Third Dynasty of Ur
entries.hint: Ur-Namma, governor of Ur, made himself king and reunited Sumer and Akkad under his city. He rebuilt the great temples and raised the first true stepped ziggurats at Ur, Uruk, Eridu and Nippur; he issued the earliest law code known; and he dug and cleared canals. He died in a battle against the Gutians, his body left on the field — a shock a Sumerian lament struggled to reconcile with divine justice.
entries.note: Frayne, RIME 3/2 (1997); the 'Death of Ur-Namma' lament translated by Jacob Klein; the law code in Martha Roth, 'Law Collections' (1997).

entries.label: Shulgi and the machine state
entries.hint: In a reign of nearly fifty years Shulgi rebuilt the state as a bureaucracy: a rotating provincial tax (the bala), a central livestock clearing-house at Puzrish-Dagan, standard weights, a fixed calendar, a courier relay, reorganised armies and a scribal school. Around year twenty he had himself declared a god. The hymns in his name praise his running, his letters, his music and his judgements; the archives his reforms generated make Ur III the best-documented state of the Bronze Age.
entries.note: Frayne, RIME 3/2 (1997); the reforms in Piotr Steinkeller, 'The Administrative and Economic Organization of the Ur III State' (1987); the Shulgi hymns edited by Jacob Klein.

entries.label: Amar-Sin and Shu-Sin
entries.hint: Under Shulgi's successors the deified-king cult reached its height — temples and statues of the living king stood in every province and received offerings. Amar-Sin campaigned in the Zagros and rebuilt Eridu. Shu-Sin built a fortified line across the waist of Mesopotamia, Muriq-Tidnim, 'the wall that keeps out the Tidnum', against the Amorite nomads pressing in from the west. It did not hold for long.
entries.note: Frayne, RIME 3/2 (1997); the wall and the Amorite pressure in Piotr Michalowski, 'The Correspondence of the Kings of Ur' (2011).

entries.label: Ibbi-Sin and the fall of Ur
entries.hint: The empire came apart around Ibbi-Sin in stages: the eastern provinces stopped sending their bala, Ishbi-Erra — an officer sent north to buy grain — set himself up as an independent king at Isin, the Amorites overran the fields, and the price of barley in Ur rose sixtyfold. In 2004 the Elamites and the men of Shimashki stormed the city, carried off the moon-god's statue, and led Ibbi-Sin in chains to Anshan. It was the end of Sumerian imperial rule.
entries.note: Piotr Michalowski, 'The Correspondence of the Kings of Ur' (2011); 'The Lamentation over the Destruction of Sumer and Ur' (Michalowski 1989).

entries.label: 'King of the Four Quarters' — the claim to universal rule
entries.hint: Naram-Sin replaced the old claim to lead 'the land' with a new one: 'King of the Four Quarters' (šar kibrāt arbaim), ruler of the whole inhabited world to its edges. Coupled with the living king's divinity, it made kingship cosmic rather than civic. Ur III revived both — Shu-Sin was a god and King of the Four Quarters — and the pairing became a template that Assyrian and Babylonian kings would reach for two thousand years later.
entries.note: Titulary in William Hallo, 'Early Mesopotamian Royal Titles' (1957); the ideology in Mario Liverani (ed.), 'Akkad: The First World Empire' (1993).

categories.label: Conflict
categories.subtitle: Sargon's conquest of Sumer, the Great Revolt against Naram-Sin, the Gutian incursions and the fall of Akkad, the Amorite wall, and the sack of Ur by Elam

entries.label: Sargon's conquest of Sumer
entries.loc: from Kish to the Lower Sea
entries.hint: Sargon defeated Lugalzagesi of Uruk in a great battle, brought him in a neck-stock to the gate of Enlil at Nippur, and then reduced the other Sumerian cities one by one — 'fifty governors', by his count — dismantling their walls and washing his weapons in the Persian Gulf. It was the first campaign to bring the whole of Sumer and Akkad under a single ruler and keep it there.
entries.note: Sargon's inscriptions in Frayne, RIME 2 (1993); narrative in Benjamin Foster, 'The Age of Agade' (2016).

entries.label: The Great Revolt against Naram-Sin
entries.hint: A coalition led by Kish and Uruk and reaching into the north and the Gulf rose against Naram-Sin. His inscriptions claim nine victories in one year and three captured kings; the Old Babylonian literary tradition made the revolt a set-piece of royal endurance. Its suppression is the event that immediately precedes Naram-Sin's deification — the king saved the city, so the city made him its god.
entries.note: The 'Great Revolt' inscriptions and their later copies in Aage Westenholz's studies; Frayne, RIME 2 (1993).

entries.label: The Gutians and the fall of Akkad
entries.hint: Through and after Shar-kali-sharri's reign the Gutians raided from the Zagros, the harvests failed, and the city of Akkad shrank and finally vanished so completely that it has never been located. The poem 'The Curse of Agade' explains the catastrophe as Enlil's revenge for Naram-Sin's supposed sacking of the Ekur at Nippur — the first attempt to give a historical disaster a theological cause.
entries.note: Jerrold Cooper, 'The Curse of Agade' (1983); the archaeology of the Akkadian collapse in Harvey Weiss's work and Foster (2016).

entries.label: Utu-hegal defeats Tirigan
entries.hint: Utu-hegal of Uruk marched out against the last Gutian king, Tirigan, praying to Inanna and to the war-god as he went, defeated him, took him and his family captive, and made him lie face down while the king set a foot on his neck. His inscription presents the victory as the liberation of the whole land and the return of kingship to Sumer.
entries.note: The Utu-hegal victory inscription in Frayne, RIME 2 (1993).

entries.label: Shu-Sin's wall against the Amorites
entries.hint: To stop the Amorite (MAR.TU) nomads filtering out of the Syrian steppe into the farmland, Shu-Sin built a fortified line, Muriq-Tidnim, running roughly between the Tigris and the Euphrates north of the cities. Garrisoning it strained the treasury, letters from the frontier officers plead for men and grain, and within a generation the Amorites were through it and inside the realm.
entries.note: Piotr Michalowski, 'The Correspondence of the Kings of Ur' (2011); the wall's route debated (Vincente; Michalowski).

entries.label: The sack of Ur
entries.hint: The collapse under Ibbi-Sin compounded: provincial defection, Ishbi-Erra's secession at Isin and his grain blackmail, Amorite raiding, famine and a sixtyfold rise in the price of barley. The finish came from the east — an army of Elam and Shimashki took Ur, burned it, plundered the temples, carried the statue of the moon-god Nanna and the king himself away to Anshan, and left a garrison in the ruins.
entries.note: 'The Lamentation over the Destruction of Sumer and Ur' (Michalowski 1989); the sequence in Michalowski, 'The Correspondence of the Kings of Ur' (2011).

categories.label: Order
categories.subtitle: The first imperial administration and the empire-wide year-name, Naram-Sin's godhood as a governing act, the Ur III command state and its bala tax, and the Code of Ur-Namma

entries.label: The first imperial administration
entries.hint: Sargon governed the conquered cities through his own appointees and 'citizens of Akkad', kept a standing corps of 5,400 men who 'ate bread daily before him', and made Akkadian the language of the chancery. The whole empire dated its documents by year-names proclaimed from the capital. It was the first working answer to the problem of ruling many cities from one — improvised, personal, and only as strong as the king.
entries.note: Benjamin Foster, 'The Age of Agade' (2016); Aage Westenholz, 'The Old Akkadian Period: History and Culture' (1999).

entries.label: Deification as a constitutional act
entries.hint: Making the living king a god was not merely flattery: it lifted him clear of the councils of city elders and the temple hierarchies that a mortal ensi had to work with, made an oath in his name a religious act, and entitled his statues to offerings. Naram-Sin's innovation gave the crown a new kind of authority, and Ur III would take it up as deliberate policy.
entries.note: Piotr Michalowski, 'The Mortal Kings of Ur' (2008); the ideological mechanics in Gebhard Selz's studies of Sumerian divine kingship.

entries.label: The Manishtushu Obelisk and the royal estate
entries.loc: Found: Susa (carried off later) · Now: Musée du Louvre
entries.hint: A four-sided stone monument records King Manishtushu buying eight large estates — thousands of hectares — from communities of landholders, paying in silver, barley, wool, oil and copper, and feasting the sellers. Whether coerced or willing, the transactions turned a patchwork of family and village land into consolidated crown estates worked by dependent labour: a lasting change in who owned Mesopotamia.
entries.note: Ignace Gelb, Piotr Steinkeller & Robert Whiting, 'Earliest Land Tenure Systems in the Near East: Ancient Kudurrus' (OIP 104, 1991).

entries.label: The bala — a command economy by rotation
entries.hint: Under Shulgi each province paid into a central pool on a fixed rota — grain, cattle, wool, reeds, craft goods, gangs of workers — and drew from it in return as the state directed. Ur and its clearing-houses matched the flows and recorded every transfer. It was a genuine planned redistribution across the whole realm, and it generated the tens of thousands of tablets that make Ur III the best-known state of the age.
entries.note: Piotr Steinkeller, 'The Administrative and Economic Organization of the Ur III State' (1987); Tonia Sharlach, 'Provincial Taxation and the Ur III State' (2004).

entries.label: The Code of Ur-Namma
entries.hint: The oldest law collection that survives opens with the king proclaiming that he has set right weights, protected the orphan from the rich and the widow from the powerful, and freed the land of tyranny — then lists some forty rulings. Many injuries are settled in weighed silver rather than by the eye-for-an-eye that Hammurabi's laws would impose three centuries later. Law is presented as a gift the just king makes to his people.
entries.note: Martha Roth, 'Law Collections from Mesopotamia and Asia Minor' (1997), pp. 13–22; first edition by Samuel Noah Kramer (1954).

entries.label: The ensi, the shagina and the audit
entries.loc: the provinces of the Ur III realm
entries.hint: Each province had two governors watching each other: a civil ensi, often local and hereditary, and a military shagina, an outsider loyal to the king. Weights, the calendar and sealed authorisations were standardised across the realm, a courier relay of ration-points moved orders and men, and every official's account was audited — a shortfall was booked against him and, if he died owing, pursued against his heirs.
entries.note: Steinkeller (1987); the audit and debt-after-death practice in Steven Garfinkle, 'Entrepreneurs and Enterprise in Early Mesopotamia' (2012).

categories.label: Belief
categories.subtitle: Ishtar the patron of Akkad, the deified living king, Enheduanna and the first authored hymns, Gudea's temple theology, and the ziggurats of the Ur III revival

entries.label: Ishtar, patron of the dynasty
entries.hint: Sargon and Naram-Sin credited their fortunes to Ishtar in her warlike aspect, Annunitum, and built her temples in the capital. Under Akkadian patronage the Sumerian Inanna and the Semitic Ishtar fused into a single supreme goddess of sexual love and of battle — the most vividly characterised deity in the Mesopotamian pantheon, and the one the empire made its own.
entries.note: Benjamin Foster, 'The Age of Agade' (2016), ch. 5; Brigitte Groneberg's studies of the goddess Ishtar.

entries.label: The living king as a god
entries.hint: From Naram-Sin, and as settled policy from Shulgi, the reigning king was a god: his name written with the divine sign, his image crowned with horns, temples and priesthoods dedicated to him, offerings burned before his statue, and ordinary people named 'Shulgi-is-my-god'. It was theology in the service of the state, and it did not survive the fall of Ur — later kings claimed divine favour, not divinity.
entries.note: Piotr Michalowski, 'The Mortal Kings of Ur' (2008); the deified-king cult in Walther Sallaberger, 'Der kultische Kalender der Ur III-Zeit' (1993).

entries.label: Enheduanna, the first named author
entries.hint: Sargon set his daughter Enheduanna over the temple of the moon-god at Ur as its en-priestess, an office that fused politics and cult. She composed a cycle of 42 hymns to the temples of the land and a long poem to Inanna in which she names herself, describes being driven from her office during a rebellion, and begs the goddess to restore her. She is the earliest author in world literature known by name — and a woman.
entries.note: William Hallo & J. J. A. van Dijk, 'The Exaltation of Inanna' (1968); Sophus Helle, 'Enheduana: The Complete Poems' (2023).

entries.label: Gudea's temple theology
entries.loc: Found: Girsu (Telloh) · Now: Musée du Louvre
entries.hint: Gudea's two clay cylinders tell how the god Ningirsu appeared to him in a dream and demanded a temple, how a goddess interpreted the dream and a god gave him the plan, and how the Eninnu was then built and consecrated, described chamber by chamber, until heaven and earth were set in order. It is the fullest surviving statement of the Mesopotamian idea that a temple is a cosmic instrument and its building a sacred duty.
entries.note: Thorkild Jacobsen, 'The Harps That Once...' (1987), pp. 386–444; Claudia Suter, 'Gudea's Temple Building' (2000).

entries.label: The ziggurat and the moon-god of Ur
entries.hint: Ur-Namma raised for the moon-god Nanna a solid stepped tower of mud brick faced in baked brick set in bitumen, its base sixty metres on a side, climbed by a triple monumental stair — the first true ziggurat, and the model for all the rest. Rebuilding Nanna's house and the ruined temples of the other cities was a founding act of the dynasty, which took the moon-god as its own.
entries.note: Leonard Woolley, 'Ur Excavations V: The Ziggurat and Its Surroundings' (1939); the Ur III temple programme in Sallaberger (1993).

entries.label: Reading the will of the gods in the liver
entries.hint: The Akkadian and Ur III periods see the first clear evidence for extispicy — putting a question to the gods, sacrificing a sheep, and reading the answer in the markings of its liver and lungs. Clay models of ominous livers and the earliest omen sentences ('if the gall-bladder is turned — the enemy will...') appear now. It became the central procedure of Mesopotamian statecraft, consulted before every campaign and appointment for two thousand years.
entries.note: Clay liver models from Mari and elsewhere; Ulla Koch, 'Secrets of Extispicy' (2005); early omens in the studies of Abraham Winitzer.

categories.label: Expression
categories.subtitle: The bronze royal head and the Victory Stele of Naram-Sin, the mythological Akkadian seal, Gudea's diorite statues, and the Sumerian literary Renaissance under Ur

entries.label: The bronze head of an Akkadian king
entries.hint: A life-size head cast in copper by the lost-wax method, the hair bound in an elaborate chignon and the beard combed into tiers of curls, the eye-sockets gouged out in antiquity to destroy its power. Long called 'the head of Sargon', it more likely shows Naram-Sin. It is the finest surviving bronze from the ancient Near East, and evidence of a foundry able to cast at monumental scale. It was stolen from the Iraq Museum in 2003 and has never been recovered.
entries.note: Iraq Museum (IM 11331); Julian Reade, 'Early Mesopotamia' (1991); the 2003 loss documented by the Iraq Museum and INTERPOL.

entries.label: The Victory Stele of Naram-Sin
entries.loc: Found: Susa (carried off later) · Now: Musée du Louvre
entries.hint: On a two-metre slab of pink sandstone, Naram-Sin — twice life-size, horned like a god — climbs a wooded mountain over the sprawled and falling bodies of the Lullubi enemy, his troops in ordered file below, the sun and stars above. It abandons the horizontal registers of all earlier relief for a single sweeping diagonal. The Elamites took it as loot to Susa around 1160 BC, adding their own inscription.
entries.note: Louvre (Sb 4); Irene Winter, 'Sex, Rhetoric, and the Public Monument' and her essays on Akkadian royal imagery.

entries.label: The Akkadian mythological seal
entries.hint: Akkadian seal-cutters set aside the crowded Early Dynastic combat-frieze for clear, deep, spacious scenes with room to breathe: the sun-god cutting his way up between two mountains at dawn, the hero Etana borne to heaven on an eagle, the water-god enthroned amid his streams, a worshipper led before a seated deity. It is the classic phase of Mesopotamian glyptic, copied and admired for the next fifteen centuries.
entries.note: Rainer Michael Boehmer, 'Die Entwicklung der Glyptik während der Akkad-Zeit' (1965); Dominique Collon, 'First Impressions: Cylinder Seals in the Ancient Near East' (1987).

entries.label: Gudea's diorite statues
entries.loc: Found: Girsu (Telloh) · Now: Musée du Louvre & dispersed
entries.hint: Some two dozen statues of Gudea survive, most of black diorite shipped from Magan — the ruler seated or standing, hands clasped, calm and heavy, in one case with the plan of a temple on his knees beside a graduated rule and a stylus. Each is inscribed with an account of the building it commemorates. They are the enduring image of the Sumerian prince as a pious steward rather than a conqueror.
entries.note: Louvre; Claudia Suter, 'Gudea's Temple Building: The Representation of an Early Mesopotamian Ruler in Text and Image' (2000).

entries.label: The Sumerian literary Renaissance
entries.hint: Ur III and the kingdom of Isin that followed gathered, edited and enlarged the body of Sumerian writing that became the classics: long hymns to Ur-Namma and Shulgi, the Gudea Cylinders, debate poems, and the copied older works. The corpus was fixed in the schools — a canon of ten core texts, the 'Decad', among them — at exactly the moment Sumerian was fading from everyday speech.
entries.note: Steve Tinney, 'On the Curricular Setting of Sumerian Literature' (Iraq 1999); Gonzalo Rubio's surveys of Sumerian literature.

entries.label: The city lament
entries.hint: The destruction of Ur produced a new literary form: the long poem in which a city's patron goddess weeps over its ruin, its people scattered, its temple defiled, its statues carried off — followed by the god's return and the city's restoration. Five great laments survive, for Ur, for Sumer-and-Ur, for Nippur, for Eridu and for Uruk. They were performed liturgically in temple ritual for a thousand years, keeping the memory of 2004 BC permanently raw.
entries.note: Piotr Michalowski, 'The Lamentation over the Destruction of Sumer and Ur' (1989); Nili Samet, 'The Lamentation over the Destruction of Ur' (2014).

categories.label: Thought
categories.subtitle: Akkadian written syllabically and the birth of the omen, the fixing of the Sumerian classics as the language died, the mature sexagesimal mathematics, and the King List as legitimation

entries.label: Akkadian written, and the birth of the omen
entries.hint: Akkadian was now written out fully, syllable by syllable, in the cuneiform borrowed from Sumerian. And alongside it grew a distinctively Mesopotamian way of knowing: collecting 'if this is observed, then that will happen' statements — from the sacrificed liver, from malformed births, from oil poured on water, from the sky — into ever-lengthening lists. The same casuistic 'if... then...' form shapes the law codes and, later, medicine and grammar.
entries.note: Francesca Rochberg, 'Before Nature: Cuneiform Knowledge and the History of Science' (2016); early omens in Ulla Koch, 'Secrets of Extispicy' (2005).

entries.label: Preserving a dying language
entries.hint: By the end of the third millennium Sumerian was becoming a language of school and office, its speakers increasingly bilingual in Akkadian and then Akkadian-speaking. The scribal establishment answered by codifying Sumerian grammar, drawing up sign-lists and vocabularies, and fixing the texts a pupil had to master. It was a deliberate act of cultural preservation, and it worked: Sumerian stayed the language of learning and liturgy in Mesopotamia for another fifteen hundred years.
entries.note: Jerrold Cooper on the 'death' of Sumerian; Niek Veldhuis, 'History of the Cuneiform Lexical Tradition' (2014).

entries.label: The sexagesimal place-value system
entries.loc: Nippur and the Ur III provinces
entries.hint: The Ur III bureaucracy had to convert, at scale and daily, between labour-days, field areas, brick counts, grain volumes and weighed silver. Out of that pressure the base-sixty place-value notation was completed — a single flexible way of writing any number, with tables of reciprocals and products to speed the arithmetic. It is the calculating engine that Old Babylonian scribes, a couple of centuries later, would push into genuinely advanced mathematics.
entries.note: Eleanor Robson, 'Mathematics in Ancient Iraq: A Social History' (2008), ch. 3; Christine Proust, 'Tablettes mathématiques de Nippur' (2007).

entries.label: Explaining the fall of Akkad
entries.hint: The collapse of the first empire set Mesopotamian scribes their first real historical question, and their answer was theological: 'The Curse of Agade' makes Naram-Sin's impious attack on Enlil's temple the reason Enlil sent the Gutians and the famine. In the same centuries the figure of Sargon became legend — the foundling drawn from a reed basket on the river, raised by a gardener, chosen by Ishtar. History was written as a lesson and a story before it was written as a record.
entries.note: Jerrold Cooper, 'The Curse of Agade' (1983); Joan Goodnick Westenholz, 'Legends of the Kings of Akkade' (1997).

entries.label: The King List as an argument
entries.hint: The Sumerian King List was compiled and revised in these centuries to make a case: that there has only ever been one kingship over the land, granted by the gods and passing from city to city — Kish, Uruk, Ur, and now (the message runs) held by the dynasty that commissioned the list. Presented as a dry chronicle of reigns, it is really a charter for the current regime's right to rule everything.
entries.note: Thorkild Jacobsen, 'The Sumerian King List' (1939); Piotr Michalowski, 'History as Charter' (JAOS 1983); Piotr Steinkeller, 'An Ur III Manuscript of the Sumerian King List' (2003).

categories.label: Economy
categories.subtitle: The imperial economy of booty and tribute, the Ur III bala redistribution and the livestock clearing-house of Puzrish-Dagan, the industrial ration system, and the grain-price collapse under Ibbi-Sin

entries.label: An empire run on booty and tribute
entries.hint: The Akkadian state lived off conquest: the plunder of defeated cities, the tribute of subject rulers, and the yield of the royal estates that Manishtushu's land purchases had built. Akkad the capital swelled as the place all of it flowed to. The Sargonic archives from Girsu, Umma, Adab and Gasur show grain, wool, copper and silver moving up to the crown's officers and out again to its soldiers and dependents.
entries.note: Benjamin Foster, 'Administration and Use of Institutional Land in Sargonic Sumer' (1982); Aage Westenholz, 'The Old Akkadian Period' (1999).

entries.label: The industrial workshop
entries.hint: Ur III ran manufactories at a scale not seen again for millennia: the weaving-houses of Ur and Lagash held thousands of women and children turning wool into graded cloth against monthly quotas, alongside milling, leather, reed and food shops. Everyone was on rations, every day's work was booked, and the overseers noted in the margin which workers had run away and which had died.
entries.note: Hartmut Waetzoldt, 'Untersuchungen zur neusumerischen Textilindustrie' (1972); Robert Englund, 'Hard Work – Where Will It Get You?' (JNES 1991).

entries.label: Puzrish-Dagan, the livestock clearing-house
entries.hint: Shulgi founded a town whose whole purpose was accounting for animals. Every province delivered sheep, goats and cattle to it — hundreds of thousands a year — and it issued them out again for temple offerings, the king's table, the messenger service and fodder, matching each transfer to the day and the responsible official. Some fifteen thousand of its tablets survive: the most exhaustive bookkeeping known from the ancient world.
entries.note: Tonia Sharlach, 'Provincial Taxation and the Ur III State' (2004); Wolfgang Heimpel and Marcos Such-Gutiérrez on the Drehem archive.

entries.label: The labour ledger
entries.hint: The state's able-bodied dependent men, the guruš, were mustered in gangs for the canals, the fields, the towpaths and the building sites, and their labour was booked like money — so many worker-days credited against a target, with shortfalls carried as a debt on the foreman's account. Sickness, flight and death were entered in the same ledgers. Work had been turned into an accountable quantity, and the worker into a line in it.
entries.note: Robert Englund, 'Organisation und Verwaltung der Ur III-Fischerei' (1990) and 'Hard Work – Where Will It Get You?' (1991).

entries.label: Silver, interest and the private operator
entries.hint: Silver by weight was the money of account and of large payment, and loans carried fixed interest — a fifth for silver, a third for barley. At the margins of the command economy stood entrepreneurs: families like Umma's 'chief merchants' who handled the state's foreign trade and internal exchanges on their own books, kept the profit on the difference, and passed the business to their sons.
entries.note: Steven Garfinkle, 'Entrepreneurs and Enterprise in Early Mesopotamia: A Study of Three Archives from the Third Dynasty of Ur' (2012).

entries.label: The grain-price collapse under Ibbi-Sin
entries.hint: As the provinces stopped delivering and the bala seized up, Ishbi-Erra — sent north with silver to buy grain — used it to establish himself at Isin and to control the supply. In Ur the price of barley rose from its normal rate to sixty times it: one of the earliest documented hyperinflations. A capital that could no longer feed its people or pay its army was finished before the Elamites arrived.
entries.note: Piotr Michalowski, 'The Correspondence of the Kings of Ur' (2011); the price data discussed by Marvin Powell and Piotr Steinkeller.

categories.label: Technology
categories.subtitle: The stepped ziggurat, monumental bronze casting, the working of imported diorite, the cadastral survey, and the state road with its relay stations

entries.label: The engineering of the ziggurat
entries.hint: Ur-Namma's ziggurat is a solid mass of millions of mud bricks wrapped in a baked-brick skin three courses thick, laid in bitumen, with reed matting and open weep-holes built into the core so rainwater could drain out rather than swell it apart. The faces are battered and very slightly convex — for stability and for the eye. Three long stairways converge at the first terrace. It was built to stand, and above all to be seen from far across the flat plain.
entries.note: Leonard Woolley, 'Ur Excavations V: The Ziggurat and Its Surroundings' (1939).

entries.label: Monumental bronze casting
entries.hint: Akkadian and Ur III founders cast large hollow figures — the royal head from Nineveh, the seated 'Bassetki statue' with its cuneiform text, the Ur III copper foundation figures of a king shouldering a builder's basket — using lost-wax and multi-part moulds. It is a command of scale and of the metal that would not be equalled in Mesopotamia for centuries afterward.
entries.note: Peter Moorey, 'Ancient Mesopotamian Materials and Industries' (1994); the Bassetki statue (found 1975; looted and recovered 2003).

entries.label: Mastering imported hard stone
entries.hint: Diorite, gabbro and dolerite — some of the hardest rock worked anywhere — were shipped from Magan and cut in the workshops of Lagash with sand-and-emery saws and bow-drills and by patient pounding, into Gudea's statues, door-sockets, stelae and heavy vessels. A land with no stone of its own had learned to import the most intractable kind and finish it to a polish.
entries.note: Peter Moorey, 'Ancient Mesopotamian Materials and Industries' (1994); the stone trade in Gudea's own inscriptions (Edzard, RIME 3/1, 1997).

entries.label: The cadastral survey
entries.hint: Ur III surveyors mapped every institutional field for the tax rolls: the plot drawn as a polygon, split into triangles and trapezoids, each piece's area worked out and the total summed and checked. Teams of 'rope-stretchers' with knotted measuring lines did the fieldwork. It is applied geometry at administrative scale — the practical mathematics on which the whole redistributive state depended.
entries.note: Mario Liverani, 'The Shape of Neo-Sumerian Fields' (BSA 1990); Jöran Friberg's studies of the Ur III field-plan texts.

entries.label: The state road and the relay
entries.loc: the routes of the Ur III realm
entries.hint: A maintained network of roads carried a chain of way-stations, roughly a day's travel apart, each stocked to feed and remount officials and couriers travelling on a sealed authorisation. The 'messenger texts' record the flour, bread and beer issued at each stop. This infrastructure — routine, unglamorous, and expensive — is what let a single city audit and direct the whole of southern Mesopotamia.
entries.note: Piotr Steinkeller, 'Corvée Labor in Ur III Times' and 'City and Countryside in Third-Millennium Southern Babylonia'; Wolfgang Heimpel on the messenger archives.

categories.label: Exchange
categories.subtitle: The ships of Magan, Meluhha and Dilmun at the quay of Akkad, the Meluhha village near Lagash, the Amorites of the western steppe, and Elam from province to destroyer

entries.label: Magan, Meluhha and Dilmun at the quay of Akkad
entries.hint: Sargon's inscription claims that ships of Magan, of Meluhha and of Dilmun moored at the quay of his capital. It is the first Mesopotamian statement of direct sea contact with the Indus valley (Meluhha), and a sign that the empire pulled the Gulf trade all the way up the Euphrates to its own centre rather than leaving it at the southern ports.
entries.note: Frayne, RIME 2 (1993); Daniel Potts, 'The Arabian Gulf in Antiquity' I (1990).

entries.label: The Meluhha village and the interpreter
entries.hint: Ur III texts mention a settlement of Meluhhans in the countryside of Lagash, its people carrying a mix of Sumerian and foreign names, and a cylinder seal names its owner 'Shu-ilishu, interpreter of Meluhhan'. An Indus-valley community was living in southern Mesopotamia, integrated enough to farm and be taxed, and distinct enough to need a professional translator.
entries.note: Simo Parpola, Asko Parpola & Robert Brunswig, 'The Meluḫḫa Village' (JESHO 1977); the Shu-ilishu seal in the Louvre.

entries.label: Magan and the copper campaigns
entries.hint: Oman — Magan — was Mesopotamia's copper mine and its source of hard diorite. Manishtushu and Naram-Sin raided across the Gulf against 'the lord of Magan'; Ur III kept up a copper trade, often brokered through Dilmun, that the Ur 'sea-faring' accounts record by weight. The metal that armed and adorned the empire came, ingot by ingot, from the far side of the Gulf.
entries.note: Frayne, RIME 2 (1993); Potts, 'The Arabian Gulf in Antiquity' I (1990); see the folio magan-3000bc-1200bc.

entries.label: The Amorites enter the record
entries.loc: the Syrian steppe and the western fringe
entries.hint: The MAR.TU or Amorites — herders of the Syrian steppe — appear now as a distinct people in the Mesopotamian sources: hired for the harvest and for military service, settling in the towns, and stereotyped in Sumerian writing as tent-dwellers 'who know no house and eat uncooked meat'. They were labour and threat at once, and by the end of Ur III a force the state could neither absorb nor keep out.
entries.note: Giorgio Buccellati, 'The Amorites of the Ur III Period' (1966); the literary stereotype in 'The Marriage of Martu'.

entries.label: Elam — from province to destroyer
entries.hint: Elam was ruled from Mesopotamia for much of this period: an Akkadian and then an Ur III governor sat at Susa, Shulgi married his daughters to Elamite princes, and a garrison held the road. The local dynast Puzur-Inshushinak broke free for a generation. And in the end it was a coalition of Elam and the Shimashki highlanders that took and burned Ur in 2004 and carried its king into captivity at Anshan.
entries.note: Daniel Potts, 'The Archaeology of Elam' (1999); Puzur-Inshushinak's inscriptions in Frayne, RIME 2 (1993).

categories.label: World
categories.subtitle: The 4.2-kiloyear drought and the emptying of the northern plains, the continuing salt in the south, and the Amorite migration into Mesopotamia

entries.label: The 4.2-kiloyear drought and the fall of Akkad
entries.loc: Tell Leilan and the Khabur plains
entries.hint: Excavations at Tell Leilan in the northern Jazira found the dry-farming settlements there suddenly abandoned around 2200 BC, under a thick layer of wind-blown dust, and stayed empty for centuries. Harvey Weiss argued this was a sharp regional aridification — the same '4.2-kiloyear event' recorded in cores worldwide — that emptied the rain-fed north, drove refugees south, and starved the Akkadian tax base. The scale of its role in the political collapse is still argued hard.
entries.note: Harvey Weiss et al., 'The Genesis and Collapse of Third Millennium North Mesopotamian Civilization' (Science 1993); the debate reviewed in Nicola Cullen et al. and in Ronald Butzer.

entries.label: The salt still rising in the south
entries.loc: the fields of Girsu and Umma
entries.hint: The Ur III agricultural records show the southern estates still managing a salinising landscape — long fallow, careful leaching, and a crop that was now overwhelmingly barley. Yields held up under intensive state management better than they had in the free-for-all of the Early Dynastic cities, but the underlying problem was not solved, only administered.
entries.note: Thorkild Jacobsen, 'Salinity and Irrigation Agriculture in Antiquity' (1982); Ur III field data in Kazuya Maekawa's studies.

entries.label: The Amorite migration
entries.loc: the western steppe and the Euphrates fringe
entries.hint: Over these centuries West-Semitic pastoralists moved steadily out of the Syrian steppe into settled Mesopotamia — seasonal grazing hardening into permanent settlement, tribal confederations (the Yamina and the Sim'al) taking shape, and Amorite men rising in the towns' garrisons and administrations. It is a slow demographic tide, and it delivers Mesopotamia's next dynasties: Isin, Larsa, Eshnunna and Babylon.
entries.note: Giorgio Buccellati, 'The Amorites of the Ur III Period' (1966); the tribal structure in Daniel Fleming, 'Democracy's Ancient Ancestors' (2004).

entries.label: The north–south hinge takes shape
entries.hint: As the far south soured under salt and the rain-fed north emptied in the drought, the strategic weight of Mesopotamia settled in the middle: Akkad, the Diyala, and the towns of the upper Tigris — Assur and Nineveh — which held Akkadian officials and then Ur III garrisons. The geography that would later carry two rival kingdoms, an Assyrian north and a Babylonian south, with the middle ground contested between them, is already visible here.
entries.note: Assur and Nineveh under Akkad and Ur III in the inscriptions (Frayne, RIME 2–3); the regional geography in Marc Van De Mieroop, 'A History of the Ancient Near East' (2016).

categories.label: Lives
categories.subtitle: The state worker driven to death in the Ur III labour rosters, the living god fed on offerings, Enheduanna in office and in exile, and the Amorite newcomer

entries.label: Worked to the ledger
entries.hint: The guruš rose to a daily muster, was set a task with a numerical quota, ate a measured ration, and had every day of his labour — and any day lost to sickness, flight or death — entered against his gang's account. Analysis of some of these rosters points to punishing conditions and a real death rate. The commonest thing a worker did to change his situation was run: the sign for 'fled', zah, is written beside many names.
entries.note: Robert Englund, 'Hard Work – Where Will It Get You? Labor Management in Ur III Mesopotamia' (JNES 1991).

entries.label: Worshipping a living man
entries.hint: With the king a god, his cult was part of ordinary life. People were given names like 'Shulgi-is-my-god' or 'Shu-Sin-is-my-help'; temples and priests of the reigning king stood in the provincial towns and received offerings; and an oath sworn 'by the king' was a religious act with a religious penalty. The state's theology reached into the household and the name a child was given.
entries.note: Walther Sallaberger, 'Der kultische Kalender der Ur III-Zeit' (1993); personal-name evidence in the Ur III onomastic studies.

entries.label: Enheduanna — office, exile and voice
entries.hint: Sargon placed his daughter at the head of the moon-god's temple at Ur to tie conquered Sumer to Akkad, and gave her a Sumerian throne-name. A rebel drove her from the office; she was later restored. What makes her unique is that she wrote about it — naming herself, describing her expulsion and her fear, and appealing to Inanna — in poems that were still being copied in the schools five hundred years later.
entries.note: William Hallo & J. J. A. van Dijk, 'The Exaltation of Inanna' (1968); Sophus Helle, 'Enheduana: The Complete Poems' (2023).

entries.label: The Amorite newcomer
entries.loc: the towns of the western fringe
entries.hint: An Amorite arriving in the Ur III world might be hired for the harvest or the garrison, be issued rations under his own name, marry a local woman, and — if he had a following — rise to command a fort or a district. He also carried the settled world's contempt: the texts jeer at the Amorite 'who digs up truffles, who does not bend his knee to farm'. Within two or three generations his kind were kings.
entries.note: Giorgio Buccellati, 'The Amorites of the Ur III Period' (1966); the stereotype in 'The Marriage of Martu' (edited by Jacob Klein).

entries.label: The slave — captive, debtor, foreigner
entries.hint: Ur III slave-sale tablets record the price of an adult at around ten shekels of silver. Slaves — war captives, purchased foreigners, and free people fallen into debt-bondage — worked in the weaving-houses and the households, could be branded and fettered if they ran, and could sometimes buy their freedom. They were a minority of the labour force, but a growing one as the interest on a bad loan pulled more of the free poor down.
entries.note: I. J. Gelb, 'Quantitative Evaluation of Slavery and Serfdom' (1979); Ur III slave sales in Bertrand Lafont & Raymond Westbrook, 'Neo-Sumerian Period' (in 'A History of Ancient Near Eastern Law', 2003).
